questions.question: In an adult who develops microangiopathic haemolytic anaemia, thrombocytopenia and acute kidney injury after sepsis, what are the major thrombotic microangiopathy syndromes that must be distinguished, and which key tests help separate TTP, STEC-HUS and complement-mediated HUS?

What clinical and laboratory features in this case supported an initial diagnosis of disseminated intravascular coagulation from severe sepsis rather than primary thrombotic microangiopathy at presentation?
Why does a normal C3 and C4 level not exclude complement-mediated haemolytic uraemic syndrome, and what does that imply for the diagnostic approach when suspicion remains high?
How should the ADAMTS13 activity result of 43.5% be interpreted in this patient, and why is the threshold of less than 10% clinically important?

The patient initially had a positive direct antiglobulin test but was later found to have 15%–20% schistocytes on smear. How do you reconcile these findings, and what clues argue for microangiopathic haemolysis rather than autoimmune haemolytic anaemia?

What is the proposed pathophysiologic link between Capnocytophaga canimorsus infection and complement-mediated HUS, and how can infection act as a trigger even in a patient without an identified pathogenic complement gene variant?

In a patient like this, why might plasma exchange be started before the diagnosis is fully clarified, and why is eculizumab considered the definitive therapy once complement-mediated HUS becomes the leading diagnosis?
What renal biopsy findings in this case supported thrombotic microangiopathy, and how did the biopsy help distinguish ongoing TMA from isolated acute tubular necrosis due to septic shock?
What infection-prevention measures are required before and after starting eculizumab, and why are these especially important in someone recovering from Capnocytophaga bacteraemia?
